checked_steps: Stay with your vehicle and try not to panic.
Before running the engine, make sure the exhaust pipe isn't blocked.
In the cold, run the engine about 10 minutes each hour for warmth, with a window open a little to keep out carbon monoxide.
Make your car easy to see: tie brightly colored cloth to a mirror, door handle or antenna.
At night, turn on the inside light while the engine is running.
In snow and wind, if you leave your vehicle you will become disoriented quickly.
After snow stops falling, raise the hood to show you need help.

Streams, rivers and other moving water can be sources of water.
Water from outdoor sources must be treated to kill germs before you drink it.
If the water might have fuel or chemicals in it, don't drink it. Boiling won't make it safe.
If the water is cloudy, first filter it through a clean cloth, paper towel or coffee filter.
Bring clear water to a rolling boil for 1 minute. Above 6,500 feet, boil it for 3 minutes.
Do not drink seawater. Drinking seawater can be deadly to humans.
Melt snow before drinking it. Eating unmelted snow will lower your body temperature.

If you are with others in a stranded vehicle, take turns sleeping.

Rest in the shade.
If you have a wide-brimmed hat, wear it to shield your face and neck from the sun.
Avoid hard activity during the hottest part of the day if you can.

message: We are camping in northern Minnesota and the sleeping bags got wet in freezing rain. Two adults, no car nearby.
checked_steps: Find shelter. Try to stay dry and cover all exposed skin.
If there's no shelter, build a lean-to or windbreak to block the wind.
If you have a wind- or waterproof jacket, wear it to keep out wind, rain and wet snow.
Wool or synthetic clothing is better than cotton. Cotton soaks up water and won't keep you warm when it's wet.
Keep your feet as dry as you can.
